# Do brief evening walks improve sleep in office workers? A randomised trial

**Abstract.** Sedentary office workers often report poor sleep. We asked whether a 20-minute evening walk improves sleep quality over four weeks. We randomised 120 office workers to a walking group (n = 60) or a stretching control group (n = 60). The primary outcome was the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI, range 0 to 21, lower is better). The walking group improved by 2.8 points more than the control group (95% CI 1.6 to 4.0, p < 0.001). The effect was smaller in participants who worked night shifts. The trial was short, and sleep was self-reported. We conclude that brief evening walks may improve sleep in day workers, and that longer trials with objective sleep measures are needed.

## 1. Introduction

Poor sleep is common among office workers and is linked to lower productivity and worse mood. Exercise is often recommended for sleep, but most trials used long sessions at a gym and few tested a short walk that fits around work. Previous reviews found small to moderate benefits, with considerable variation between studies. We therefore tested a 20-minute walk, because a short, low-cost habit is more likely to be kept.

## 2. Methods

We recruited 120 adults from three offices in one city between March and May. Eligible people worked at a desk for at least six hours a day and had a baseline PSQI score above 5. Participants were randomised by a computer to either a 20-minute walk within two hours of leaving work, five evenings a week, or a 20-minute stretching routine on the same schedule. Walkers were asked to keep a gentle pace. Both groups kept a short diary. The primary outcome was the change in PSQI score from baseline to week 4. We used a linear model adjusted for baseline score and shift pattern. Twelve participants (10%) did not complete week 4 and were analysed as randomised, using multiple imputation.

## 3. Results

The mean baseline PSQI score was 9.1 in the walking group and 9.0 in the control group. After four weeks the walking group had improved by 3.9 points and the control group by 1.1 points, a difference of 2.8 points (95% CI 1.6 to 4.0, p < 0.001). Among the 18 participants who worked night shifts, the difference was 0.9 points (95% CI -1.3 to 3.1). Adherence was high: walkers completed a median of 17 of the 20 planned walks. No adverse events were reported.

## 4. Discussion

A short evening walk improved self-reported sleep more than stretching over four weeks. The size of the difference is similar to that seen in longer programmes. The smaller effect in night-shift workers fits the idea that the timing of exercise relative to the body clock matters, but the subgroup was small and this analysis was not planned in advance.

### Limitations

The trial lasted only four weeks, so we cannot say whether the benefit lasts. Sleep was self-reported and neither group was blinded to its activity. All participants came from three offices in one city, so the result may not apply to other groups.

## References

Smith et al. (2019). Exercise and sleep: a review. Sleep Medicine Reviews.
